opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think a lot of it comes down to information density. Text is this incredibly compressed representation of human thought. When somebody writes a sentence, they've already done a huge amount of work distilling what matters. So every token you train on carries a lot of signal about how people reason, what they know, and how the world works. With images, you've got millions of pixels, and most of them are telling you that the sky is blue or the wall is beige. There's a lot less meaning per bit.

There's also a practical side. The internet is full of text, it's cheap to store, cheap to process, and the training objective is very clean: predict the next word. That one simple objective turns out to force the model to learn grammar, facts, reasoning, even a bit of common sense, because to predict well you have to understand what's going on.

And then there's what you get out of it. Language is the interface to basically everything people do. If a model can read and write, it can answer questions, write code, explain things, carry on a conversation. That's enormously useful right away, which means people use it, which funds more research and more compute. It's a nice flywheel.

Images and video and other modalities absolutely matter, and models are getting very good at them. But if you're asking where the intelligence comes from, I'd say text was the natural starting point, because that's where humanity has written down most of what it knows.

r001.rationale: The response describes text as a compressed representation with high signal per token, while images have many pixels and less meaning per bit.

r002.rationale: It notes that text is plentiful online, but does not identify fewer human-produced image examples as a training-data disadvantage for image generation.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think text is just the most information-dense signal we have about how humans think. People wrote down pretty much everything they know, and they did it in a form that's already compressed. A picture is a million pixels, and most of those pixels are telling you very little. A sentence is a few dozen tokens and it can carry a whole idea. So if you want to learn reasoning, world knowledge, how concepts relate to each other, text is where that's sitting out in the open.

And there was a practical side to it too. The amount of text on the internet was enormous, and it was cheap to get and cheap to process. In the early days compute was the real constraint, and text just gave you more learning per flop than anything else. You could train a language model on a few GPUs and watch it get better in a way that was measurable. Perplexity was a nice clean number. With images it took a lot longer before the generative side looked good enough that anybody cared.

I also think text happened to match the Transformer really well. Sequences of discrete tokens, attention over positions, next-token prediction as the objective. It's a very simple recipe, and that simplicity meant you could scale it without inventing a lot of new machinery. And once the models could talk, they became useful immediately. You could ask one a question and get an answer. That's a product. Image generation is wonderful, but a model that can read and write is a model you can actually collaborate with, and I think that's why the whole field converged there first.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts a sentence of a few dozen tokens carrying a whole idea with an image’s million pixels, most of which convey little, identifying text as more information-dense per raw representation.

r002.rationale: The response cites abundant, cheap internet text as a practical advantage, but does not identify a lack of human-produced image examples as a training-data disadvantage for image generation.

astra-6.text:
Text is a very convenient place to start because it’s already discrete. You’ve got this sequence of symbols, and you can give the model a very simple task: predict the next one. There’s a huge amount of text available, and people have packed a lot of knowledge into it—facts, explanations, arguments, code. So getting good at predicting text pushes you toward learning a lot about the world.

Images are also incredibly valuable, but you’re dealing with a lot of detail that may not matter for what you’re trying to understand. Text has already had a human do some of that compression for you. Someone decided what was important and put it into words. That makes it a particularly useful starting point.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts text’s human-compressed, meaningful content with images’ excess detail, conveying that text carries more useful information in a compact representation.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention a shortage of examples of humans producing images or identify that as a training-data disadvantage.

sol-6.1.text:
Text is a very convenient place to start because it’s already digital, it’s relatively compact, and there’s a huge amount of it. You can also get a training signal almost for free: hide the next word and ask the model to predict it. You don’t need somebody to label every example.

And language contains a lot of information about the world. To predict what somebody is going to say, you have to learn something about what they know, what they’re trying to do, and how things work. So this very simple objective can push you toward fairly general capabilities. Images are a natural thing to learn from too, but text gives you a particularly convenient combination of data, computation, and a useful training objective.

r001.rationale: The response calls text “relatively compact” but does not say it carries more information than images for the same amount of raw data.

r002.rationale: It does not mention a shortage of examples of humans producing images or identify that as a disadvantage for training image-generation models.
